name: Squalane
lead: Squalane is a saturated hydrocarbon (C30H62) made by hydrogenating squalene, a lipid found in human sebum, shark liver oil, olives and some other plant sources. It is a colourless, odourless, lightweight oil used mainly as an emollient and skin-conditioning ingredient in moisturisers, serums and hair products.[1][2]

In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a gentle, non-greasy moisturiser and as a vehicle in skincare products. Published research on squalane itself as a cosmetic active is sparse: most of the literature concerns squalene and squalane as vaccine adjuvant components, as drug-delivery vehicles and as skin-barrier lipids.[2][3] One small randomised trial tested a fullerene-in-squalane cosmetic against wrinkles, but it did not isolate squalane's own effect.[4]

Reviews describe emollient and skin-hydrating activity for squalene and squalane, largely from in vitro and animal work.[2] Squalane is sold over the counter in cosmetic products and appears in some US-listed topical product labels.[5]
infobox: Plant-derived (olive, sugarcane) or historically shark liver oil[1][6]

paras: Squalane is the fully hydrogenated form of squalene, a branched 30-carbon triterpene hydrocarbon. Removing squalene's double bonds makes the molecule more resistant to oxidation, which is the main reason the saturated form is used in finished cosmetics.[1] Human sebum naturally contains squalene (roughly 13 percent in one review), while squalane itself is a manufactured or isolated derivative.[2]

Historically squalane was obtained from deep-sea shark liver oil. Reviews on squalene supply note ecological concerns about shark harvesting and describe plant-derived and fermentation-based sources as alternatives; current cosmetic squalane is commonly marketed as olive- or sugarcane-derived.[1][6][7]

Squalane is used as an emollient in moisturisers, facial oils, serums, lip and hair products. Product descriptions and secondary sources characterise it as lightweight, quickly absorbed and suitable for oily or acne-prone skin, although these properties are asserted mainly in cosmetic-industry and general-reference descriptions rather than in controlled trials of squalane alone.[1][2]

A topical product label listing squalane with niacinamide in a dark-spot corrector advises external use only, avoiding the eyes, discontinuing if irritation occurs and using sunscreen during the day.[5]

Squalane and squalene emulsions are used as oil components of vaccine adjuvants and as drug-delivery vehicles; this is a separate, well-documented use unrelated to appearance.[3][8][9] Squalane-containing adjuvants were also tested in an early malaria sporozoite vaccine trial.[10]

Stratum corneum lipids are an important determinant of the skin's water-holding function, and experiments replenishing sebum-derived lipids on lipid-depleted human skin found recovery of water-holding properties.[11][12] Squalane is an occlusive, lipid-like hydrocarbon, and reviews credit squalene and squalane with hydrating and emollient effects in animal and in vitro models.[2] An ex vivo study of squalane-based emulsions examined their influence on skin penetration of polyphenols.[13]

Squalane and squalene have been the subject of a safety review in the International Journal of Toxicology (2023).[14] General-reference descriptions report low irritation potential at cosmetic concentrations and recommend patch testing for sensitive individuals.[1] No notable adverse-event literature specific to topical squalane is available in the reviewed sources.

Controlled human studies of squalane as a standalone cosmetic active are scarce. A randomised controlled trial reported in 2010 evaluated fullerene-C60 dissolved in squalane as an anti-wrinkle cosmetic; because the active comparison was the fullerene preparation, it does not establish an effect of squalane alone.[4] Other human work involves squalane as an adjuvant component in vaccines rather than as a skin product.[10]

card.summary: Shelf-stable, lightweight moisturising oil made from squalene; widely used in skincare, with little trial data of its own.
card.note: Evidence for appearance benefits rests mostly on general emollient science and product descriptions, not squalane-specific trials.

quick.overview:
Squalane is a stable, oily hydrocarbon made by hydrogenating squalene, a lipid that also occurs in human skin oil. It is sold as a lightweight moisturiser or ingredient in serums, facial oils and hair products.

It is described as non-greasy and suitable for many skin types, but those descriptions come largely from general references and cosmetic marketing. Few controlled trials have tested squalane on its own.
quick.mechanism: As an emollient and occlusive lipid it is thought to help the skin retain water; reviews report hydrating and emollient activity mainly from animal and laboratory work, and lipid-replacement studies in human skin show barrier lipids affect water-holding.
quick.risks: Reviewed sources describe low irritation potential and generally recommend patch testing for sensitive skin. It is a cosmetic ingredient sold over the counter. Sourcing differs between plant-derived and historically shark-derived material.
